hints: Look at the scale bar under the capillary. It tells you the real-life diameter is only 7 µm, but the drawing on the page is much bigger. Grab a ruler and measure that same diameter on the page in mm.
Remember magnification = image size divided by actual size, but both must be in the same units. Convert your mm measurement to µm first using 1 mm = 1000 µm.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image and get units matching**

Great start, this is a classic magnification calculation. Measure the diameter of the capillary drawing on your paper, you should get about 35 mm.

Now convert to micrometres so it matches the actual size:
$$1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$$
$$35 \text{ mm} \times 1000 = 35000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$$

**Apply the magnification formula**

Magnification tells us how many times bigger the image is than real life:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$
Put in your numbers:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{35000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}}{7 \text{ } \mu\text{m}} = 5000$$

**Conclude with confidence**

So the drawing is 5000 times larger than the real capillary. That makes sense because a capillary lumen is tiny, about the width of a red blood cell, so we need huge magnification to see it clearly.

options.A: Too small. At x200 the image would be only 1.4 mm wide, much smaller than the drawing you see.
options.B: Too small. This value comes from forgetting to convert mm to µm correctly.
options.C: Too small by a factor of 10. This is a common slip when converting mm to µm using 100 instead of 1000.
options.D: Correct. Image size of about 35000 µm divided by actual size of 7 µm gives x5000.
